title: The Difficult Promise of a Cubic Carrier

scenes.text: A cubosome is no solid cube. A continuous lipid bilayer separates two intertwined water channels. Geometry alone proves nothing about delivery.
Water-soluble cargo enters channels; lipophilic cargo associates with the bilayer. An imaging label can accompany the carrier without sharing the drug's fate.
Particle size cannot establish cubic structure. Small-angle X-ray scattering identifies lattice order, with cryogenic microscopy providing complementary structural evidence.
An imaging signal can locate a labeled carrier. The drug must also be released and reach its biological target. These are different measurements.
Blood proteins change a particle's biological identity. Distribution becomes complex; a targeting ligand alone cannot demonstrate selective delivery to tumors.
A bright scan may coexist with declining available drug. This is conceptual, not measured data. Calibration is essential before inferring drug exposure.
Our chapter separates carrier localization, release reporting, pharmacodynamic effects, and calibrated signal-to-exposure relationships. Each level demands stronger evidence.
Structural stability, manufacturing consistency, biodistribution, and safety remain formidable hurdles. Promising cells and beautiful microscopy cannot establish clinical efficacy.
The promise is an image that reveals meaningful treatment exposure. Until that link is validated, cubic geometry remains a beginning, not an outcome.
